facts.statement: Lithornis is an extinct genus of paleognathous birds.
facts.quote: Lithornis is a genus of extinct paleognathous birds.

facts.statement: Lithornis was capable of good flight, despite being closely related to modern flightless ratites and poor-flying tinamous.
facts.quote: Although Lithornis was able to fly well, their closest relatives are the extant tinamous (which are poor flyers) and ratites (which are flightless birds).

facts.statement: Lithornis fossils are confirmed from the Upper Paleocene to the Middle Eocene, with a possible extension into the late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Fossils of Lithornis are known with certainty from the Upper Paleocene through the Middle Eocene, but their fossil record may extend to the late Cretaceous.

facts.statement: The name Lithornis means 'stone bird' in ancient Greek, reflecting its early prominence in fossil bird discussions.
facts.quote: Lithornis is from ancient Greek for 'stone bird', as it is one of the first fossil birds to become widely discussed.

facts.statement: Richard Owen described the species Lithornis vulturinus in 1840 based on bones resembling those of vultures.
facts.quote: L. vulturinus was described as having vulture-like bones by Richard Owen in 1840 from the holotype fossil 955 738 - TM 024 717.

facts.statement: The type fossils of Lithornis vulturinus were collected from Early Eocene London Clay deposits on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent, England.
facts.quote: They were collected from Early Eocene London Clay deposits on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent, England

facts.statement: The original holotype fossil of Lithornis vulturinus was destroyed during bombing in World War II.
facts.quote: This fossil was destroyed by bombing in World War II.

facts.statement: A neotype was designated in 1988 to replace the destroyed holotype, allowing researchers to diagnose the genus as a paleognath based on North American congeners.
facts.quote: A neotype (BMNH A 5204) was erected to replace the holotype in 1988 by Houde, who for the first time diagnosed it as a paleognath based on complete three-dimensional skulls and skeletons of congeners from North America.

facts.statement: Lithornis possessed wing bones similar to storks and vultures, enabling it to soar, unlike its modern tinamous relatives.
facts.quote: Lithornis' wing bones are similar to those of storks and vultures, meaning that unlike modern tinamous it was capable of soaring flight.

facts.statement: Lithornis had well-developed olfactory lobes suggesting a nocturnal, forest-dwelling lifestyle, while retaining large optical lobes common in flying birds.
facts.quote: In a study about ratite endocasts, Lithornis ranks among the taxa with well developed olfactory lobes. This is consistent with a nocturnal, forest-dwelling lifestyle, though as much all volant birds it retains large optical lobes.

facts.statement: Lithornis had toe claws and reversed halluxes that allowed for efficient perching, a trait not found in modern tinamous.
facts.quote: Unlike modern tinamous, Lithornis has toe claws and reversed halluxes that allow for efficient perching.

facts.statement: Some researchers classify the genus Calciavis as a species of Lithornis, specifically L. grandei.
facts.quote: Some researchers consider Calciavis as a species of Lithornis (L. grandei).

facts.statement: Lithornis lived between 60.9 and 48.07 million years ago, from the Selandian to the Ypresian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Selandian to Ypresian (60.9 to 48.07 million years ago)

facts.statement: Lithornis belongs to the family Lithornithidae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Lithornithidae

facts.statement: The species Lithornis celetius was described by Peter Houde in 1988 from fossils found at Bangtail Quarry in Montana.
facts.quote: L. celetius is from the Bangtail Quarry, Sedan Quadrangle, Park County, Montana, and was described by Peter Houde (1988).

facts.statement: Lithornis celetius lived during the earliest Tiffanian stage of the Late Paleocene, as indicated by the Fort Union Formation.
facts.quote: It is from the Fort Union Formation, which is earliest Tiffanian, Late Paleocene.

facts.statement: Lithornis celetius was of average size for the genus, and its name references a race horse from the type locality.
facts.quote: L. celetius was of average size for the genus, and the name Celetius is derived from the Greek word keletion a race horse for which the type locality is also named.

facts.statement: The species Lithornis hookeri was originally described as Pediorallus hookeri in 1984 before being transferred to the genus Lithornis.
facts.quote: In 1984, Harrison redescribed the fossil as coming from a new species Pediorallus hookeri, and later that year it was moved to Lithornis hookeri.

facts.statement: Lithornis hookeri is the smallest species within the family Lithornithidae.
facts.quote: L. hookeri is the smallest of the Lithornithidae.

facts.statement: The original fossil for Lithornis nasi was collected by W. George from the London Clay at Walton on the Naze, Essex, England.
facts.quote: W. George collected the original fossil in the Division A London Clay, North Sea Basin at Walton on the Naze, Essex, England.

facts.statement: Lithornis nasi was originally described as the rail Pediorallus nasi by Harrison in 1984 before being reclassified.
facts.quote: The fossil was described by Harrison in 1984 as a rail, Pediorallus nasi, but was later moved to Lithornis nasi.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Lithornis nasi is a distinct species or a junior synonym of L. vulturinus, with recent studies arguing for its distinctness based on size differences.
facts.quote: In 2015, L. nasi was proposed to be a junior synonym of L. vulturinus because its differences in shape and size from the latter species were concluded to more likely represent intraspecific variation. Mayr and Kitchner (2025) disagreed with the proposed synonymy based on their notable size difference.

facts.statement: Lithornis promiscuus was described by Peter Houde in 1988 from the Willwood Formation in Wyoming, dating to the earliest Eocene.
facts.quote: L. promiscuus has type specimen USNM 336535 and was described by Peter Houde (1988). It is from the Clark Quadrangle, Park County, Wyoming, USA. It is from the Willwood Formation, which is earliest Eocene in age.

facts.statement: A fossil egg attributed to Lithornis celetius has been identified.
facts.quote: An egg, USNM 336570, is known for L. celetius as well.

rejected.statement: Fossil eggshells attributed to Lithornis are described as being 'ratite-like'.
rejected.quote: Several egg fossils have been attributed to Lithornis. Their eggshells are, perhaps unsurprisingly, noted as being 'ratite-like'.
